segments.translit: tam evārthaṃ gabhīradharmmādhigamena siddhācāryyo hi d[ā]rikaḥ pratipādayati —
segments.translation: Through his realization of the profound [dharma]{dharma}, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Dārika]{p-darika} sets forth that same meaning:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song: the siddha (an accomplished tantric adept) Dārika, having realized the profound dharma, sets out 'that same meaning' already taught (cp.34.m1).

segments.translit:
sunakaruṇetyādi | karuṇeti saṃvṛtisatyaṃ śūnyam iti | tasya pariniṣṭhitarūpaṃ paramārthasatyaṃ | ubhayam abhedopacāreṇa gṛhītvā vajraguruprasādāt siddhācāryyo hi dārikaḥ | gagaṇam iti ālokādiśūnyatrayaṃ boddhavyaṃ tasya pāraṃ prabhāsvaro mahāsukhena pariśuddhakāyavākcittāvirbhā(bhā)vaniyamena vilasati |
tathā cāgamaḥ —
bhāvebhyaḥ śūnyatā nānyo na ca bhāvo 'sti tāṃ vinetyādi | [50ka]
segments.translation:
'[Emptiness]{sunyata} and [compassion]{karuna}…' and so on. '[Compassion]{karuna}' is [conventional]{samvrti} truth. '[Emptiness]{sunyata}' is its perfected form, [ultimate]{paramartha} truth. Taking the two together by applying [nondifference]{abheda} to them, through the [grace]{prasada} of the [vajra]{vajra} [guru]{guru}, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Dārika]{p-darika} (the '[sky]{gagana}' is to be understood as the [three emptinesses]{sunyatraya} beginning with [light]{aloka}, and its [far shore]{para} is [clear light]{prabhasvara}) is at [play]{lila} with [great bliss]{mahasukha}, by the rule of the manifestation of purified [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}.
And so the [scripture]{agama} says:
'Emptiness is not other than things, nor is there a thing without it,' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta reads compassion as conventional truth and emptiness as its perfected form, ultimate truth; by the vajra guru's grace Dārika takes the two as non-different. The sky is the three emptinesses beginning with light, its far shore clear light, where he plays in great bliss through purified body, speech and mind (cp.34.m2).

equations.en: ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), the perfected form of the conventional
the three emptinesses beginning with light (ālokādiśūnyatraya)

citations.quoted: bhāvebhyaḥ śūnyatā nānyo na ca bhāvo 'sti tāṃ vinā
citations.work: Unnamed: introduced only as 'scripture' (āgama); not identified here

flags.note: Where the Sanskrit glosses compassion as conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya), the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'conventional bodhicitta' (kun rdzob byang chub kyi sems); its gloss of emptiness as ultimate truth (don dam pa'i bden pa) agrees. The Tibetan may reflect a text reading saṃvṛtibodhicitta, or the translators' own gloss. I translate the Sanskrit.

Shastri prints the daṇḍa after śūnyam iti ('karuṇeti saṃvṛtisatyaṃ śūnyamiti | tasya…'). I divide after saṃvṛtisatyaṃ, so that 'śūnyam iti' opens the gloss of emptiness as the perfected form of the conventional. The Tibetan divides the same way (stong pa zhes pa ni de yongs su rdzogs pa'i gzugs don dam pa'i bden pa'o).

In 'tasya pāraṃ prabhāsvaro', prabhāsvaraḥ is masculine nominative while pāram is neuter, so the word could instead describe Dārika ('luminous, he is at play beyond it'). I follow the Tibetan (de'i pha rol 'od gsal ba, 'its far shore, clear light') in taking the far shore as clear light. The sentence is also broken: Dārika is the subject of vilasati, and the glosses of sky and far shore stand between them; the parentheses in the translation mark that.

Shastri prints pariśuddhakāyavākcittāvirbhā(bhā)vaniyamena, with a doubled syllable; I read āvirbhāva, 'manifestation': 'by the rule of the manifestation of purified body, speech and mind'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) differs twice: 'wholly filled (yongs su gang ba) with great bliss', as if reading paripūrṇa for pariśuddha, and 'by the certainty that body, speech and mind are free of own nature' (lus dang ngag dang yid rnams rang bzhin dang bral ba'i nges pas), as if the compound held a word for absence (abhāva) rather than āvirbhāva. The doubled bhā might conceal such a reading.

In the scriptural verse the manuscript has nānyo; the sense needs nānyā, agreeing with śūnyatā. The Tibetan (dngos po rnams las stong pa nyid / gzhan dngos gnas pa ma yin no) gives the same sense loosely.

vajra (keep-source-first-gloss) first occurs in this unit here, in 'vajra guru'. Suggested short gloss: the thunderbolt-diamond, emblem of the indestructible; as a prefix it marks what belongs to the tantric path, so the vajra guru is the tantric master who gives empowerment and instruction.

segments.translit:
dhruvapadena tam evārthaṃ draḍhayati —
alakham iti | ata eva anutpādena lakṣyate cittam alakṣyaṃ tena prabhāsvare citte na vilasati sugama[ṃ] paraṃ |
segments.translation: With the [refrain]{dhruvapada} he makes that same meaning firm: '[Mark of the unmarkable]{alaksya-laksana}…': for this very reason the [mind]{citta}, which cannot be marked, is marked by [non-arising]{anutpada}. By that he is at [play]{lila} in the [mind]{citta} that is [clear light]{prabhasvara}. The rest is easy.
segments.note: Munidatta reads the refrain as making the first couplet's meaning firm: the mind cannot be marked, yet non-arising marks it, and so Dārika plays in the mind that is clear light. The printed Sanskrit says he does 'not' play; the Tibetan has no negative, and the negative is set aside here (cp.34.m3).

equations.en: the mind, which cannot be marked, marked by non-arising (anutpāda)

flags.note: The printed Sanskrit reads 'tena prabhāsvare citte na vilasati', 'therefore he does not play in the mind of clear light'. I translate without the negative. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'de yis 'od gsal ba'i sems kyis rnam par rol par byed', 'by that he plays with the mind of clear light', with no negative; the refrain being glossed says Dārika plays (bilasai); and in cp.34.m2 Munidatta himself says vilasati. The na may be a slip (for sa, 'he'?) or the remains of mahāsukhena, which would gloss the refrain's mahāsuhe as in cp.34.m2 ('mahāsukhena … vilasati'). If the printed text is kept, the sentence reads 'Therefore he does not play in the mind of clear light' (cp.34.m3).

Munidatta closes with his formula 'sugamaṃ param', 'the rest is easy' (cp.34.m3). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has instead 'bde ba'i pha rol du 'gro ba'o', 'goes to the far shore of bliss': the translators seem to have taken sugama as 'going well' (su- rendered bde ba, as in sugata, bde bar gshegs pa) and param as pāram, 'far shore'. I keep the formula.

For 'anutpādena lakṣyate cittam alakṣyaṃ' the Tibetan has 'ma skyes pa mtshan nyid med pa sems kyi mtshan nyid do', 'the unborn, without characteristics, is the characteristic of mind': the same sense, put as a definition.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadenānyaṃ saṃbodhayati —
kinto ityādi | manteneti bāhyamantrajāpena | re vaṭa bālayogin | kiṃ tava tanteneti tantrapāṭhena ca dhyānavyākhyānena vā kim | apratiṣṭhānamahāsukhalīlayā tava nirvvāṇaṃ durlakṣyaṃ gurucaraṇareṇukiraṇaprasādāt prasiddham eva |
tathā ca sarahapādāḥ —
manta na tanta na ityādi |
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he addresses another: 'What use…' and so on. '[Mantra]{mantra}' means the recitation of outer mantras. 'Hey' means 'O [lad]{vatu}, [novice yogin]{balayogin}!' 'What use to you is [tantra]{tantra}' means: what use is reading the tantras, or [concentration]{dhyana} and [exposition]{vyakhyana}? Through the [play]{lila} of [non-abiding]{apratisthana} [great bliss]{mahasukha}, your [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}, [hard to discern]{durlaksa}, is fully accomplished by the [grace]{prasada} of the rays of the dust of the [guru]{guru}'s feet.
And so [Saraha]{p-saraha} says:
'No mantra, no tantra…' and so on.
segments.note: Munidatta takes the couplet as addressed to another, a novice yogin: reciting outer mantras, reading tantras, concentration and exposition are no use. Through the play of non-abiding great bliss, where the song says 'absorbed', the nirvāṇa hard to discern is accomplished by the grace of the guru's feet. He cites Saraha's 'no mantra, no tantra' (cp.34.m4).

citations.work: Saraha (named by Munidatta); probably from his Dohākoṣa, not checked

flags.note: Munidatta's 'apratiṣṭhānamahāsukhalīlayā', 'by the play of non-abiding great bliss' (cp.34.m4), stands where the song has apaiṭhānamahāsuhalīṇe, 'absorbed in non-abiding great bliss'. It may be his own reading of līṇe as līlā, or a scribal change from a form of līna. The Tibetan comment has 'rab tu mi gnas pa'i bde ba chen por thim pa'i phyir', 'because of dissolving into non-abiding great bliss', and its line has thim; both support the song's līṇa, 'absorbed'. I translate the Sanskrit as printed.

The Sanskrit says that with this verse the poet addresses another (anyaṃ saṃbodhayati); the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'gzhan ma yin par 'bod par byed', 'calls out to one not other' (or 'not to another'), as if reading ananyaṃ, or dividing dvitīyapade nānyaṃ. I keep 'another': Munidatta's own vocative, 'O lad, novice yogin', and his 'your nirvāṇa' address someone other than the poet (cp.34.m4).

The Tibetan cites Saraha's line as 'sngags dang rgyud', 'mantra and tantra', without the negatives of 'manta na tanta na'; probably just abbreviation. It renders vaṭa bālayogin as byis pa rmongs pa'i rnal 'byor pa, 'childish, deluded yogin'.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena mārgasyānuśaṃsām āha —
duḥkheti | duḥkheneti paramārthasatye(ttvo)na saha ekīkṛtya bho bālayogin guru[ṃ] pṛṣṭvā viṣayendriyopabhogaṃ kuru | etadupāyena sakalānuttaraṃ gatvā dāriko hi siddhācāryyaḥ saṃsāre svaparāparaṃ vibhāgaṃ bhedaṃ na paśyatīti |
tathā ca dhokaṛipādāḥ —
saṃsāre [51] bahu saṃsaranti sudhiyo eṣa prabhāve 'pi ca |
bhāvābhāvayuge vicāryya sakalaṃ svaprajñayā (prajñāya) saṃsthitam |
pakṣyāpakṣyam avekṣa vādigaditaṃ pakṣaṃ na paśyāmy ahaṃ
grāhyagrāhakavarjjitaṃ hi munibhiḥ duḥkhaiḥ yathā[saṃ]tataṃ ||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he speaks the [praise]{anusamsa} of the [path]{marga}: 'Suffering…' 'With suffering' means: having made it one together with [ultimate]{paramartha} truth, and having asked the [guru]{guru}, O [novice yogin]{balayogin}, enjoy [sense objects]{visaya} and [senses]{indriya}. By this [means]{upaya}, having gone to the [unsurpassed]{anuttara} of all, the [siddha]{siddha} master [Dārika]{p-darika} does not see in [saṃsāra]{samsara} any division, any difference, of [self and other]{sva-para} or not-other.
And so [Dhokaṛipāda]{p-dhokari} says:
'The wise wander much in [saṃsāra]{samsara}, and by the [power]{prabhava} of this too
everything in the pair of [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava}, on [examination]{vicara}, stands firm in one's own [wisdom]{prajna}.
Looking at [side]{paksa} and not-side, I do not see the side that disputants proclaim;
for it is free of [the grasped and the grasper]{grahya-grahaka}: by the sages, with sufferings, just as it ever runs on.'
segments.note: Munidatta calls this couplet praise of the path: suffering is made one with ultimate truth, and the novice yogin, after asking the guru, is to enjoy sense objects and senses. By this means Dārika has gone to the unsurpassed of all and sees no division of self and other in saṃsāra. He adds a verse of Dhokaṛipāda (cp.34.m5).

equations.en: having made it one together with ultimate truth (paramārthasatyena saha ekīkṛtya)

citations.quoted: saṃsāre bahu saṃsaranti sudhiyo eṣa prabhāve 'pi ca | bhāvābhāvayuge vicāryya sakalaṃ svaprajñayā saṃsthitam | pakṣyāpakṣyam avekṣa vādigaditaṃ pakṣaṃ na paśyāmy ahaṃ grāhyagrāhakavarjjitaṃ hi munibhiḥ duḥkhaiḥ yathā[saṃ]tataṃ
citations.work: Dhokaṛipāda (named by Munidatta); the work is not named and is not identified here

flags.note: The Sanskrit introduces couplet 4 as the 'third verse' (tṛtīyapadena), following Munidatta's count, which leaves out the refrain (cp.34.m5). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'second verse' (rkang pa gnyis pas). Since the Tibetan itself calls couplet 3 the second verse (cp.34.m4, rkang pa gnyis pas) and couplet 5 the fourth (cp.34.m6, rkang pa bzhi pas), its 'second' here is probably a slip for gsum pa, 'third'.

Read strictly, 'duḥkheneti paramārthasatyena saha ekīkṛtya' glosses 'with suffering' by 'together with ultimate truth', which could equate suffering itself with ultimate truth (as cp.34.m2 equates emptiness with it); I translate 'having made it one together with ultimate truth', leaving the object open. The Tibetan adds a gloss the Sanskrit lacks, 'sdug bsngal ni 'khor ba'i bde ba dang sdug bsngal', 'suffering is the happiness and suffering of saṃsāra', which is then made one with ultimate truth; a phrase may be lost from the Sanskrit.

Shastri prints paramārthasatye(ttvo)na, offering an alternative in parentheses (apparently -sattvena or -tattvena). The Tibetan don dam pa'i bden pas, 'with ultimate truth', supports satyena. Where the Sanskrit has the novice yogin first ask the guru (guru[ṃ] pṛṣṭvā, with Shastri's restored ṃ), the Tibetan has 'bla ma'i drin la', 'through the guru's kindness'.

What Munidatta's wording implies for the song (cp.34.m5; the draft is not changed). 4a: 'viṣayendriyopabhogaṃ kuru', 'enjoy sense objects and senses', stands where the song has bhuñjai indījānī. He takes bhuñjai as enjoyment (upabhoga) and indījānī through indriya, 'sense', as he takes indiāla in song 30 (cp.30.m4), not as indrajāla, 'magic show'; and he turns the line into an instruction to the novice yogin. The Tibetan line, 'mig 'phrul dra ba za bar byed', 'eats the magic net', supports the draft. 4b: 'sakalānuttaraṃ gatvā', 'having gone to the unsurpassed of all', implies he took saalānuttaramāṇī as reaching an unsurpassed state, not as deeming all things unsurpassed. The Tibetan line, 'ma lus bla na med par shes', 'knows all as unsurpassed', supports the draft's sense of māṇī; the Tibetan comment has 'all became unsurpassed' (thams cad bla na med par gyur pa).

svaparāparaṃ: I keep the draft's 'self and other or not-other' (apara as a-para). The Tibetan comment lists three, 'rang dang pha rol dang gzhan', 'self, other and another', and its line has 'rang gzhan gzhan nyid'; 'another' is also the commoner Sanskrit sense of apara. Munidatta's 'vibhāgaṃ bhedaṃ', 'division, difference', does not decide it (cp.34.m5).

Dhokaṛipāda's verse is in śārdūlavikrīḍita and is corrupt in places. Line 1: 'eṣa prabhāve 'pi ca' does not construe (nominative eṣa with locative prabhāve); I follow the Tibetan, 'di yi mthu yis, 'by the power of this'. Line 2: the metre needs svaprajñayā, not Shastri's alternative (prajñāya). Line 3: pakṣyāpakṣyam avekṣa stands for pakṣāpakṣam avekṣya; the Tibetan has 'I did not see anything at all' (bdag gis cung zad kyang ni ma mthong) for 'I do not see the side', and 'speaking' (smra gyur pa) for 'proclaimed by disputants'.

Line 4 of the verse, 'grāhyagrāhakavarjjitaṃ hi munibhiḥ duḥkhaiḥ yathā[saṃ]tataṃ', is obscure as printed, and my rendering is literal ('free of the grasped and the grasper: by the sages, with sufferings, just as it ever runs on'). The Tibetan reads 'gzung ba dang ni 'dzin pa spangs pa'i phyir / dga' dang sdug bsngal ji bzhin de nyid do', 'since grasped and grasper are given up, joy and suffering are just as they are', as if it had a word for joy where the Sanskrit has munibhiḥ, and yathā saṃsthitam, 'as it stands', for Shastri's restored yathā [saṃ]tataṃ; the metre allows yathā saṃsthitam. That reading would tie the verse to the song's making suffering and happiness one.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena svakīyānuśaṃsām āha —
rāā ityādi | uktitrayeṇa svakīyaṃ kāyaiśvaryyādikaṃ guṇaṃ sūcitaṃ | anye ye devā nāgendrādayo viṣayamohena baddhās tiṣṭhanti | vayaṃ punar lūyīpādaprasādāt dvādaśabhūmino jinasamāḥ | 34 |
segments.translation: With the fourth [verse]{pada} he speaks his own [praise]{anusamsa}: '[King]{raja}…' and so on. By the threefold utterance his own qualities, beginning with lordship of the body, are indicated. Those others who are gods, lords of [nāgas]{naga} and the like remain bound by [delusion]{moha} about [sense objects]{visaya}. We, however, by the [grace]{prasada} of [Lūyī]{p-luyi}pāda, hold the [twelve stages]{dvadasa-bhumi} and are equal to the [Jinas]{p-jina}. (34)
segments.note: Munidatta hears the triple 'king' as the poet's praise of his own qualities, beginning with lordship of the body. The other kings are gods, lords of nāgas (serpent beings) and the like, bound by delusion about sense objects; 'we', by Lūyīpāda's grace, hold the twelve stages and equal the Jinas. He does not enumerate the twelve (cp.34.m6).

equations.en: the threefold utterance, pointing to the poet's own qualities, beginning with lordship of the body (kāyaiśvarya)
the others: gods, lords of nāgas (nāgendra) and the like, bound by delusion about sense objects

flags.note: On the twelve: the song has dvādaśabhuaṇem̐, literally 'in twelve worlds' (bhuaṇa from bhuvana, as in tiṇi bhuaṇa, 'three worlds'). Munidatta renders it with bhūmi, 'stage' (cp.34.m6): dvādaśabhūminaḥ, 'possessed of the twelve stages', and adds jinasamāḥ, 'equal to the Jinas'. He does not enumerate the twelve or say how they relate to the usual ten bodhisattva stages. The Tibetan line has sa bcu, 'ten stages', perhaps normalizing to the familiar ten; the Tibetan comment has sa bcu gnyis pa'i rgyal ba, which can mean 'the Jinas of the twelve stages' or 'the Jina of the twelfth stage', so the comment keeps Munidatta's twelve against its own line.

For 'kāyaiśvaryyādikaṃ guṇaṃ', 'qualities beginning with lordship of the body', the Tibetan has 'rang gi bya ba dbang phyug la sogs pa'i yon tan', 'his own activity, lordship and other qualities', perhaps reading kārya for kāya. It renders vayaṃ punar, 'we, however', as bdag ni slar yang, 'I, again'.

questions: cp.34.m3: I translated Munidatta's 'tena prabhāsvare citte na vilasati' without the negative ('by that he is at play in the mind that is clear light'), on the Tibetan (rnam par rol par byed, no negative), the refrain's own bilasai and his vilasati in cp.34.m2. Do you want the printed 'does not play' in the text, with the emendation moved to a note?

cp.34.m5, for the song draft (not changed here): Munidatta's 'enjoy sense objects and senses' (viṣayendriyopabhogaṃ kuru) takes 4a's indījānī through indriya, not indrajāla, and his 'having gone to the unsurpassed of all' (sakalānuttaraṃ gatvā) takes 4b's saalānuttaramāṇī as reaching a state, not 'deeming all unsurpassed'. The Tibetan lines support the draft (mig 'phrul dra ba; ma lus bla na med par shes). Should 4a and 4b each carry a note giving his reading?

cp.34.m5: Dhokaṛipāda's verse is corrupt in lines 1 and 4. I kept line 4 literal and flagged the Tibetan's 'joy and suffering are just as they are'. Would you rather the English follow the Tibetan sense there, marked as an emendation?

cp.34.m6 and 5b: Munidatta reads bhuaṇa as bhūmi, 'stage', and does not enumerate the twelve; the Tibetan line has sa bcu, 'ten stages', its comment sa bcu gnyis pa. The approved 'twelve stages' follows him. Should the note on 5b say that the song literally has 'twelve worlds' (compare tiṇi bhuaṇa, 'three worlds')?

cp.34.m5 and 4b: for svaparāpara the draft has 'self and other or not-other', which I kept; the Tibetan line (rang gzhan gzhan nyid) and comment (rang dang pha rol dang gzhan) read three terms, self, other and another. Is 'not-other' the reading you want?
cp.34.m2: I took 'tasya pāraṃ prabhāsvaro' as 'its far shore is clear light', with the Tibetan and the glossary, though the masculine prabhāsvaraḥ could describe Dārika ('luminous'). Agreed?
